spec.title: Board Specifications
items: 2-layer PCB
Maximum board size 100mm x 100mm
FR-4 material, 1.6mm thickness
1 oz copper weight

spec.title: Component Placement
items: Place STM32F405RGT6 MCU in the center of the board
Group decoupling capacitors close to power pins of ICs
Place crystal oscillator and its load capacitors close to MCU

spec.title: Power Supply
items: Separate power planes for 24V, 5V, and 3.3V
Wide traces for power connections (min. 20 mil)
Place DC-DC converter and LDO with proper thermal considerations

spec.title: Signal Integrity
items: Keep high-speed signals (e.g. SPI, UART) short and direct
Use ground planes to reduce EMI
Avoid 90 degree angles in traces, use 45 degree or curved traces

spec.title: CAN Interfaces
items: Route CAN differential pairs close together
Maintain 100-ohm differential impedance for CAN traces (suggested)
Place 0 ohm resistors for CAN linking in accessible locations

spec.title: Connectors
items: Use connectors for all interfaces
Place connectors along the board edges for easy access

spec.title: GPIO Expansion
items: Route GPIO expansion ports as connectors
Clearly label all GPIO ports on the silk screen

spec.title: Pneumatic Control
items: Use 2 pin port for pneumatic control
Clear label of polarity

spec.title: Indicators and Interfaces
items: Place LED indicators in a visible area of the board
Group SWD, UART, and TFT interface connectors logically

spec.title: Mechanical Considerations
items: Include 4 mounting holes, one near each corner of the PCB
Ensure components clear the mounting holes

spec.title: Silk Screen and Labeling
items: Clearly label all connectors and major components
Include board name, revision, and date on silk screen

spec.title: Design for Manufacturing
items: Maintain minimum 10 mil trace width and spacing
Use standard drill sizes

spec.title: Grounding
items: Implement a solid ground plane
Use stitching vias to connect top and bottom ground planes

spec.title: Testing and Debug
items: Place all buttons in an accessible location

categories.name: Trace Routing
categories.blurb: How you draw the copper decides whether the board survives the fab and carries its current without cooking itself.

examples.title: 45° corners everywhere
examples.description: Every bend in a trace is a 45° cut or a smooth curve. No trace on the board turns a hard right angle.
examples.reason: Sharp corners trap etching chemicals, which eat the copper thin right at the bend. On fast signals they also throw the impedance off. Two 45° bends (or an arc) cost nothing and avoid both.

examples.title: Trace widths from net classes
examples.description: Power nets run at 0.5 mm, signals at 0.25 mm — set once in net classes, so the design rule check flags any trace that breaks them.
examples.reason: Rules in the checker beat rules in your head. Widths stay consistent across the whole board, and anyone can verify the setup in one place.

examples.title: Teardrops where traces meet pads
examples.description: Every trace flares out into a smooth teardrop before it reaches its pad — no skinny trace walking straight into a big pad.
examples.reason: A thin trace meeting a large pad concentrates stress at the junction — that's where copper lifts when you rework a joint or the board flexes. The flare spreads the load over more copper so the connection stays put.

examples.title: 90° corners on traces
examples.description: One or more traces turn a hard right angle.
examples.reason: Acid trap: etching fluid pools in the corner and eats the copper thin exactly where the trace bends. On fast signals the corner also adds capacitance and bounces energy back. Two 45° bends fix it for free.

examples.title: Traces that neck down
examples.description: A trace squeezes thinner than its class width to slip between two pads.
examples.reason: The thin part carries the same current as the rest of the net — it becomes a fuse you didn't ask for, heating first and sometimes vanishing during etching. If it won't fit at full width, move the pads.

examples.title: Leftover stubs on a net
examples.description: A trace branches and one arm goes nowhere — a dead-end stub, usually left behind after a reroute.
examples.reason: At speed, an open stub rings and radiates — a little antenna you didn't order. When a net moves, delete the old copper. Don't leave tails.

examples.title: Placement first, snapped to a grid
examples.description: Every part is placed and signed off before a single trace is routed — parts snapped to a 0.5–1 mm grid, lined up in tidy rows.
examples.reason: Routing a bad placement is just decorating a mistake. When parts sit on a grid the short, obvious routes appear by themselves, and the board reads like it was drawn on purpose.

examples.title: Route power first, then the fussy nets, then the rest
examples.description: Routing happens in order: power rails and high-current paths first, then CAN/USB/clock, then everything else.
examples.reason: The leftovers always find a way around — the rails and the fast nets won't. If you route signals first you'll keep cutting them up to make room for copper that needed to be there all along.

categories.name: Power & Grounding
categories.blurb: Clean power in, heat out, joints that actually solder. This is where boards live or die.

examples.title: Thermal relief on plane pads
examples.description: Any pad that connects into a copper plane does it through four spokes — never solid copper.
examples.reason: A solid link into a big plane pulls heat away faster than the iron can put it in — hello, cold joints. Spokes keep the connection while letting the pad get hot enough to solder.

examples.title: Ground stitched through vias
examples.description: Top and bottom ground pours are tied together with stitching vias — thickly near anywhere a signal swaps layers.
examples.reason: Stitching gives return currents a short way home. Short loops mean less noise, and the planes stop ringing against each other at RF.

examples.title: Use polygon for connecting high current power rail
examples.description: Top and bottom ground pours are tied together with stitching vias — thickly near anywhere a signal swaps layers.
examples.reason: With a wider polygon pour, the current density is lower, which reduces the voltage drop and heat generation. It also provides a larger area for heat dissipation and improves the overall reliability of the power rail.

examples.title: One decoupling cap per power pin
examples.description: Every VDD / VDDA / VBAT pin on the MCU gets its own 100 nF cap with a short path to the pin and to ground. Our usual way: a 3.3 V zone on the back layer, each cap via'd straight down into it.
examples.reason: Each pin draws its own bursts of current, and only a cap sitting right next to it can answer fast enough. The back-layer zone keeps the return paths short without eating up the top side.

examples.title: Regulators dump heat through vias
examples.description: The regulator's tab / exposed pad is stitched with thermal vias down to the ground plane. The plane's copper does the spreading.
examples.reason: The tab is the part's main heat exit. Vias into ground copper turn the whole plane into a heatsink — for our loads, that's plenty.

examples.title: Power rails run on copper, not wire
examples.description: The 5 V output reaches its inductor through a pour, the LM1117's 3.3 V leaves on a zone, and the 3.3 V rail is zoned or fat — never signal-width. Bulk caps sit next to the load, beside the inductor.
examples.reason: Rails carry the whole board's current, so thin wire means lost voltage and heat where you can least afford it. Copper is free — spend it. On the switcher side, fat copper also keeps the noisy loop tight.

examples.title: Via drilled inside an SMD pad
examples.description: A via sits inside an SMD pad, untented and unplugged.
examples.reason: During reflow, liquid solder drains down the via and starves the joint — or the lopsided pad flips the part upright (tombstoning). Keep vias outside pads, or use properly filled and plugged via-in-pad.

examples.title: Copper pour flooding a pad
examples.description: A ground pour has crept onto a signal pad with no clearance.
examples.reason: That's a short to the plane — sometimes one you only find after assembly, when the board is already full of parts. Every pour obeys the clearance rule on every net. No exceptions.

examples.title: One cap shared across power pins
examples.description: A single cap — or a bunch tied together — feeds two or more of the MCU's power pins.
examples.reason: The shared cap sits too far from most pins, and its path crosses everyone else's return current — so noise flows through the whole bunch instead of dying at its source. One pin, one cap, short path.

examples.title: Every IC gets its own decoupling
examples.description: Not just the MCU — motor drivers, CAN transceivers, sensor ICs, anything with a power pin gets a 100 nF cap right at that pin.
examples.reason: Each chip switches its own current and needs its own local reservoir. A driver pulling amps for a motor is exactly the part you don't want borrowing the MCU's cap. One cap per power pin, on every chip.

examples.title: Bulk cap at the entry, ceramic at the pin
examples.description: A big electrolytic (10–47 µF) sits near where power comes in, and small ceramics sit at each IC — they work as a team.
examples.reason: The bulk cap is the slow, deep tank that soaks up big draws; the ceramic is the quick one that answers in nanoseconds. One without the other leaves a gap. Big at the door, small at the pin.

examples.title: Power rails drawn as thin traces
examples.description: A regulator feeding its inductor through a skinny trace, or the 3.3 V rail routed at signal width.
examples.reason: Thin copper on a rail means voltage drop and heat under load. On the switcher side it also stretches the loop, which makes ringing worse. If a rail must cross busy territory, pour it on another layer and stitch down — don't thin it out.

examples.title: 22 pF where the regulator wants 22 µF
examples.description: The regulator's bulk cap fitted in the wrong size class — a pF value where µF is needed.
examples.reason: A pF cap only filters the very fastest noise; the bulk cap is the energy bucket the load drinks from. With a pF in its place the output sags and the regulator can ring under load. Read µF / nF / pF twice on every part before ordering.

examples.title: Reverse-polarity protection on the power entry
examples.description: Every battery / supply input has a series diode or P-MOSFET so a reversed plug or battery does no damage.
examples.reason: Reversed power is the fastest way to kill a board, and it will happen — connectors are small and pits are dark. A single cheap part turns a dead board into a “flip the plug” moment.

examples.title: A fuse on the battery feed
examples.description: A polyfuse or proper fuse sits in series with the main battery input, sized just above the board's normal draw.
examples.reason: Wiring mistakes, a jammed motor, a shorted tool on the bench — all of them pull huge current. The fuse gives up before the trace or the battery connector does, and a polyfuse resets itself after the fault is removed.

categories.name: High-Current Design
categories.blurb: Amps don't care how hard you tried — high-current paths want copper area and short loops, not long skinny traces.

examples.title: 45 degree corners everywhere
examples.description: Every change of direction is a 45 degree mitre or a smooth arc, no net on the board carries a right angle.
examples.reason: Right-angle corners trap etchant during fabrication and become impedance bumps on fast signals. 45 degree corners etch evenly, keep impedance constant and read as intentional work.

examples.title: Width by rail: 80 / 30 / 20 / 10 mil
examples.description: 24V runs at about 80 mil, 5V at 30 mil, 3.3V at 20 mil, and signal wires at 10 mil, all set once as net classes.
examples.reason: These are the team's working numbers for this board's current budget. Rails too thin sag and heat, signal wires too fat just waste room. When in doubt, go one step wider on power, copper is free.

examples.title: 90 degree corners on traces
examples.description: One or more traces turn with a sharp right angle.
examples.reason: Acid trap: etchant pools inside the corner and over-etchs the copper, thinning the trace exactly where it bends. On fast signals the corner adds capacitance and reflects energy. Use two 45 degree segments or an arc instead.

examples.title: Vias aligned, spaced, other side checked
examples.description: Use vias to hop layers instead of long detours, placed in neat rows with space between them, after checking the far side isn't already occupied.
examples.reason: A via landing on a pad, trace or part on the other layer is a hidden short or a broken net. Line them up on-grid, give each one breathing room, and flip the view before you drop them.

examples.title: Leftover stubs off the main run
examples.description: Dead-end copper branches left hanging off a net after a reroute.
examples.reason: Stubs are antennas: they reflect energy back into fast signals and pick up noise on sensitive ones. After every reroute, delete the old copper, a clean net has exactly one path.

categories.name: Power & Grounding
categories.blurb: Clean power delivery and joints that can actually be soldered, the difference between a board and a paperweight.

examples.title: One decoupling cap per power pin
examples.description: Every VDD, VDDA and VBAT pin of the MCU gets its own 100 nF cap with a short path to the pin and to ground.
examples.reason: Each pin draws its own switching current, and a dedicated local cap is the only reservoir close enough to answer. The back-layer zone keeps every return path short without burning routing space on top.

examples.title: Thermal relief on plane connections
examples.description: Every pad tied into a copper plane connects through four spokes, never solid copper.
examples.reason: A solid tie into a big plane drags heat out of the joint faster than the iron can deliver it, the classic cold joint. Spokes keep the electrical connection while letting the pad reach soldering temperature.

examples.title: Copper pour floods a pad
examples.description: A ground pour creeps onto a signal pad with zero clearance.
examples.reason: That is a short between the pad and the plane, sometimes only visible after assembly, when the board is already populated. Every pour must respect the board clearance rule against every net, no exceptions.

examples.title: Regulator outputs leave on copper zones
examples.description: The 5V switcher output reaches its inductor through a pour, the LDO's 3.3V leaves on a zone, and the 3.3V rail itself is zoned or fat, never signal width.
examples.reason: Rails carry the whole board's current, so thin wire drops voltage and burns heat exactly where you can least afford it. Copper is free, spend it. On the switcher side, wide copper also keeps the commutating loop tight and less noisy.

examples.title: One decoupling cap shared across power pins
examples.description: A single cap, or a bunch wired together, feeds two or more VDD pins of the MCU.
examples.reason: The shared cap sits too far from most pins, and its path crosses everyone else's return current, so noise flows through the whole bunch instead of dying at its source. One pin, one cap, short path.

categories.name: CAN, Clock & Signals
categories.blurb: CAN bus, crystal and general signal routing, the small grouping and placement decisions that decide whether the bus survives a noisy robot.

examples.title: CANH and CANL as symmetrical as possible
examples.description: The two CAN wires run grouped with the same length, the same bends and the same spacing, as close to a mirror image as the board allows.
examples.reason: CAN rejects noise by seeing it equally on both wires. The more symmetric the pair, the more noise arrives as common mode and gets cancelled. Lightly grouped is the floor, mirror-symmetric is the goal.

examples.title: Load caps first, then the crystal
examples.description: Both load caps sit between the MCU and the crystal, at the same distance from it, with equal-length stubs to ground.
examples.reason: The caps have to shunt the crystal pins to ground, any trace past the cap toward the crystal detunes the load capacitance. Placing the two caps as mirror images keeps both sides of the oscillator equally loaded.

examples.title: CAN lines routed independently
examples.description: CANH and CANL sent on separate paths, or one of them crossing a power or switching area alone.
examples.reason: Whatever couples into one line but not the other arrives as a differential error, the one kind of noise CAN cannot reject. Re-pair them, even loosely, and steer both wires around the noisy copper.

examples.title: Signals crossing a plane split
examples.description: A fast net routed straight over a gap or split in the ground plane beneath it.
examples.reason: Signal current goes out on the trace and comes back directly underneath it, on the plane. When the plane is split there's no path back, so the return detours around the gap, making a big loop that radiates and picks up noise.

categories.name: Footprints & Packages
categories.blurb: The footprint is a promise to the assembly house. Break it and the part simply will not fit.

examples.title: Library footprints, IPC-7351
examples.description: Every part uses a footprint from the team library, generated to IPC-7351 density level B.
examples.reason: Generated footprints match real part bodies and paste-stencil rules, avoiding the tombstoning and misalignment that hand-drawn pads cause after reflow.

examples.title: Mirrored footprint
examples.description: A part drawn as if seen through the board, pads mirrored, silkscreen text backwards.
examples.reason: The component physically cannot be placed. This happens when a footprint is edited in the wrong layer view, so flipping the view is the very first thing anyone checks.

examples.title: Headers packed with no room for housings
examples.description: Adjacent 4-pin or 2-pin headers spaced for bare pins only, XH housings and plugs have nowhere to go.
examples.reason: XH housings are wider than their pins, and plugs need approach space. Pack headers together and only the first one stays pluggable. Space them for the housings, not for the drill holes.

examples.title: Mounting holes done properly
examples.description: Four plated mounting holes, one near each corner, with a keep-out ring of silk and copper clearance.
examples.reason: The hole is half the job, the other half is the space above it for the screw head and washer. A part parked under a screw is a part that gets cracked at assembly.

categories.name: Silkscreen & Documentation
categories.blurb: The board must be readable by a human holding a soldering iron at 2 a.m. before a competition.

examples.title: Header legends: function first, then pins
examples.description: Every header's silk names the function first, then the per-pin map, e.g. UART_VRTG means UART, and from left to right: 5V, RX, TX, GND.
examples.reason: A port labelled J4 tells you nothing in the pit. UART_VRTG tells you what it is and what every pin does without opening the schematic. Function first, detail second, read left to right.

examples.title: Silkscreen over pads
examples.description: Legend lines or text cross exposed copper pads.
examples.reason: Ink on a pad stops solder from wetting, opens and weak joints follow. Many fabs silently strip silk from pads, taking your markings with it. Keep all silk at least 0.2 mm from exposed copper.

examples.title: Board name, rev and date on the silk
examples.description: Every board carries its name, document revision and date in a silkscreen corner.
examples.reason: Six months from now, three board revisions will live in the same drawer. The silkscreen is the only way to tell them apart without a microscope and a prayer.

categories.name: Clearance & DFM
categories.blurb: Respect the fab's minimums and the physics of high voltage, the board has to survive manufacture and the real world.

examples.title: DRC clean at the fab's real limits
examples.description: The design passes DRC with zero errors, the RDC baseline is 10 mil trace and spacing.
examples.reason: A clean DRC at the fab's actual capability is the cheapest insurance that exists. Running it with looser rules just hides failures the fab will find for you, at your expense.

examples.title: Copper slivers between pads
examples.description: Thin copper splinters left between pads after a pour flood.
examples.reason: Slivers can detach during etching and bridge neighbouring pads, or corrode loose months later. Adjust pour clearance and hunt for isolated islands after every flood.

examples.title: Creepage violation on HV nets
examples.description: Mains or high-voltage nets run closer than the creepage table allows.
examples.reason: Too little surface distance lets tracking arcs form across the board over time, a safety failure, not a cosmetic one. HV nets get their own clearance rules and usually a routed slot.

categories.name: Deliverables
categories.blurb: What you hand over, and in what state. A perfect layout with broken outputs is still an incomplete submission.

examples.title: Gerber set verified in a viewer
examples.description: All copper layers, masks, silks, paste, outline and the Excellon drill file exported, then eyeballed layer by layer in a Gerber viewer before zipping.
examples.reason: Viewer review catches missing layers, mirrored art and wrong units before the board ships. Most 'the fab broke my board' stories start exactly here.

examples.title: Missing or mismatched drill file
examples.description: The drill file is absent from the Gerber zip, or drill hits do not line up with the pads.
examples.reason: Without the drill data nobody can make holes, or worse, the fab guesses. Re-export the whole set from one CAD session and verify every layer, every time.

checklist: Board is 2-layer, 100mm x 100mm max, FR-4 1.6mm per spec
DRC passes with zero errors at the fab's real limits
No right-angle corners, acid traps or leftover stubs on any net
Widths by rail: 24V ~80 mil, 5V ~30 mil, 3V3 ~20 mil, signal ~10 mil
One 100 nF decoupling cap per power pin of every IC
Thermal relief on plane pads, regulator tab via'd to GND copper
No vias inside untented SMD pads
CANH/CANL symmetrical, same length, same bends
Crystal caps mirrored on the MCU side, caps before the crystal
Pin-1 and polarity marked on every polarised part
Header legends show function plus pin map
Connectors from the library with 3D checked, spaced for housings
4 mounting holes, one per corner, clear of components
Gerber set and drill file verified layer-by-layer in a viewer
